current_answer: A 4% AI job-loss number is a 2030 model scenario, not a count of jobs already gone. A new CEPR paper maps assumed AI-capability paths into three futures; its ‘substantial change’ scenario has cognitive employment 4% lower by 2030 and is consistent with median U.S. survey expectations. The sharpest observed warning remains narrower: smaller Danish firms that reported AI use in 2023 later had 11% slower employment growth, driven by recruitment. That association is not causal or universal. U.S. exposure-based studies still show mixed early-career and posting signals; there is no measured economy-wide layoff verdict.

catalogue_card.question: Is the 4% AI jobs figure a measured result?
catalogue_card.text: No. It is a conditional 2030 model scenario. The strongest observed warning is still slower hiring at some Danish AI adopters—not a count of jobs already erased.

summary: The CEPR paper’s 4% cognitive-employment decline belongs to one 2030 scenario, not a measured job-loss result today.
The sharpest observed warning remains slower recruitment and employment growth at smaller Danish firms that reported AI adoption; the study does not establish cause or a universal effect.

Broad U.S. and Nordic counter-signals still block an economy-wide layoff verdict. The next test is whether observed firm adoption changes hiring, pay, separations and unemployment across comparable firms.
uncertainty: The CEPR scenario depends on assumed capabilities, automation and reallocation, and it assigns no probability to the illustrated paths.
The Danish adoption study is an association in one country; adopters can differ from other firms before and after reported use.
U.S. early-career and posting studies use exposure and different outcomes, leaving remote work, education, pre-trends and other explanations unresolved.
No current study can predict a reader’s own job loss or prescribe a career decision.
freshness_note: Checked 20 September 2026. A new 2030 employment scenario changes how a precise AI job-loss number must be read; it does not add a measured economy-wide job-loss result.
